new.definition: A loose French custard of cream, milk and egg yolks, baked gently until just set and served in the small pot or ramekin it was baked in. The name means pot of cream, and in French kitchens crème also means custard. It is softer and lighter than crème brûlée, made with less cream and finished with no burnt sugar crust, and it is eaten with a spoon from its pot, never turned out. On the Thanksgiving Day menu it was the Sweet Potato Pot de Crème, with miso, cinnamon and marshmallow fluff.
new.guest: A pot de crème, said poh duh KREM, is a silky French custard, baked gently and served in the little pot it set in; the name means pot of cream. Ours on Thanksgiving Day was made with sweet potato, with a touch of miso, cinnamon and marshmallow fluff: the holiday casserole remade as a French custard.
new.kitchen: The custard is baked low and gently, usually in a water bath, and taken out while the center still trembles, because too much heat curdles the egg and makes the custard grainy and weeping. How the house set the sweet potato custard, and how the fluff was finished, was the kitchen’s to say at lineup.
new.compare: Crème brûlée is its nearest neighbor: both are baked custards served in their dish, but crème brûlée is richer, heavier in cream and yolk, baked in a wider, shallower ramekin and topped with a crust of burnt sugar. A pot de crème is softer and has no crust. Crème caramel, the third of the family, is the one turned out onto the plate in its own caramel.

new.background: Pot de crème is French for pot of cream, and in French kitchens crème serves for custard as well as for cream, so the name says custard in its pot. The name belongs as much to the vessel as to the dessert: it was made and served in a small porcelain cup, often lidded. French porcelain makers turned out such cups in the eighteenth century. The Cooper Hewitt, Smithsonian Design Museum holds a soft paste porcelain custard pot made at Mennecy around 1770, and notes that the French name for custard, crème anglaise, means English cream, and that the cup was made while the French fashion for all things English was in full swing. In most kitchens today a plain ramekin stands in for the lidded pot. At Brennan’s on Thanksgiving Day the custard was made with sweet potato.

new.definition: Egg cooked gently in milk or cream until the egg proteins set the liquid. Stirred over low heat it stays pourable and is crème anglaise; baked, usually in a water bath, it sets firm enough to spoon or slice, as in pot de crème, crème brûlée and crème caramel. In a milk and egg custard the proteins thicken at about 79 to 83 C (175 to 185 F), and only a few degrees past that they tighten into curds and squeeze out water. On the Thanksgiving Day menu it was the base of the Sweet Potato Pot de Crème, and a French style vanilla ice cream is a stirred custard churned and frozen.
new.guest: A custard is simply eggs cooked gently in milk or cream until they set it, silky rather than firm. Our Sweet Potato Pot de Crème on Thanksgiving Day was a baked custard, made with sweet potato and served in its little pot. A French style vanilla ice cream is a custard too, churned as it freezes.
new.kitchen: Gentle heat is the whole craft: a stirred custard comes off the heat as it coats the back of a spoon, and a baked one comes out of its water bath while the center still trembles, since a few degrees too many make it grainy and weeping. Whether the vanilla ice cream with the Bananas Foster starts from a custard base is the kitchen’s to confirm.
new.compare: Its two forms are the first tell: a stirred custard, crème anglaise, pours, while a baked custard holds its shape in the dish. In ice cream the egg is the tell: French style ice cream is a custard with egg yolks, dense and smooth, while Philadelphia style has no egg and freezes icier.

new.background: The word custard began as the name of a pie, not of its filling. Middle English crustarde or crustade meant a dish baked in a crust, from Latin crusta, crust. The Forme of Cury, the roll of recipes compiled about 1390 and credited to the master cooks of Richard II (1367 to 1400), gives crustardes of meat and of fish, pies in which beaten eggs strained through a cloth are poured over the filling before baking. By the early 1600s the word had slipped from the crust to the creamy egg filling itself. French cooks came to call the stirred version crème anglaise, English cream, and that same stirred custard, churned as it freezes, is the base of a French style ice cream.

new.definition: A Japanese paste of soybeans fermented with salt and koji, the mold Aspergillus oryzae grown on rice, barley or the soybeans themselves. Shiro, or white, miso is fermented for a shorter time with a higher share of koji, so it is mild and sweet; aka, or red, miso ferments longer and is darker, saltier and stronger. A spoonful brings salt and deep savory flavor, umami, to soups and glazes and, in pastry, to caramel and baked sweets. On the Thanksgiving Day menu it was the savory note in the Sweet Potato Pot de Crème.
new.guest: Miso, said MEE-soh, is a Japanese fermented soybean paste. A little in a dessert works much as the salt does in a salted caramel: it brings a savory depth that makes the sweetness taste rounder. In our Sweet Potato Pot de Crème it sat with cinnamon and marshmallow, so the custard was never simply sweet.
new.kitchen: Pastry cooks reach for white miso in sweets and use it sparingly, cutting back the other salt, because too much overwhelms the sugar. Which miso the house used, and whether it went into the custard or a caramel, was the kitchen’s to say; miso is soy, so every soy question goes to the kitchen.
new.compare: Soy sauce is its nearest neighbor, a seasoning of the same fermented soybean family: soy sauce is a thin liquid you pour, miso a thick paste you stir in. Among misos, color is the tell: the paler the miso, the milder and sweeter it is.

new.background: Miso grew from the fermented seasonings of China, which the Japanese called hishio, though when and how it reached Japan is disputed: one account carries it with Buddhism in the sixth century, and Japan’s agriculture ministry records a theory that it came from the Korean kingdom of Goguryeo in 666. The first written record in Japan is the Taihō Code of 701, which names it misho, a word unknown in China, read as not yet hishio. The paste is made by mixing cooked soybeans with salt and koji, the mold Aspergillus oryzae, and leaving it to ferment, and the length of that rest and the share of koji give the many regional misos their colors and strengths. Far from Japan, pastry cooks have taken mild white miso into sweets, most often as miso caramel, for its salt and savory depth.

new.definition: A brand of marshmallow creme: soft, spoonable whipped marshmallow sold in jars, made since 1920 by Durkee-Mower, a Massachusetts candy firm. Its jar label has listed corn syrup, sugar, dried egg white and vanillin, with no gelatin, so it gets its lift from whipped egg white rather than the gelatin of a marshmallow. It is sweet, sticky and light. On the Thanksgiving Day menu it went with the Sweet Potato Pot de Crème, a nod to the sweet potato casserole under marshmallows.
new.guest: Marshmallow Fluff is marshmallow creme in a jar, a New England sweet since 1920: soft, whipped marshmallow made with egg white. On our Sweet Potato Pot de Crème it was a wink at the sweet potato casserole with marshmallows that so many families bake for Thanksgiving.
new.kitchen: Whether the house used the jarred brand or whipped its own marshmallow, and whether it was toasted, was a question for lineup. Marshmallow creme carries egg white, so egg questions go to the kitchen with every other allergy question.
new.compare: A marshmallow is its nearest neighbor: a marshmallow is set firm with gelatin, so it can be cut and holds its shape, while the creme stays soft and spoonable, lifted by egg white, and carries no gelatin.

new.background: Marshmallow takes its name from a plant, the marsh mallow, Althaea officinalis, whose root sap French confectioners of the nineteenth century whipped with sugar and egg white into a soft paste, pâte de guimauve; gelatin later took the place of the root and gave the firm marshmallow. Marshmallow Fluff came from the soft side of that family. Archibald Query (1873 to 1964), a confectioner of Somerville, Massachusetts, made a marshmallow creme in his kitchen in 1917 and sold it door to door until the sugar shortages of the World War I years set his trade back. Two veterans of that war from Swampscott, who formed a partnership to make Fluff in 1920, bought his formula, and their firm, Durkee-Mower, which moved to a factory in Lynn in 1929, built the brand. Earlier marshmallow cremes did exist, so Fluff was not the first, but it is the name that stuck.

new.definition: The sweet, starchy root of Ipomoea batatas, a vine of the morning glory family native to the tropical Americas. The orange fleshed kinds Louisiana grows are moist and sweet when cooked, where some older eastern kinds are drier and paler. In Louisiana they are sold as yams, though a true yam is a different plant altogether. On the Thanksgiving Day menu it filled the Sweet Potato Agnolotti and flavored the Sweet Potato Pot de Crème.
new.guest: Sweet potatoes are a Louisiana crop, and here people often call them yams, though botanically they are no yam at all. On Thanksgiving Day we used them twice: inside the agnolotti, with brown butter, candied pecans and goat cheese, and in a silky pot de crème, the holiday casserole turned into a custard.
new.kitchen: Where the house sweet potatoes came from, and what went into the agnolotti filling with them, was the kitchen’s to say; the sheet printed neither, so ask before calling them Louisiana grown.
new.compare: The true yam is its nearest neighbor in name only: a yam is a Dioscorea, of a different plant family altogether, while a sweet potato belongs to the morning glory family. An orange fleshed yam in a Louisiana market is a sweet potato.

new.background: The sweet potato is native to the tropical Americas and was domesticated there, in Central or South America, thousands of years before Europeans arrived. Louisiana grows it as a field crop, and in the 1930s the state’s growers began selling their moist, orange fleshed roots as yams, to set them apart from the drier, paler sweet potatoes grown further east. The name stuck, though botanically a yam is another plant. Louisiana State University’s sweet potato breeding began in that decade, and in 1987 the LSU AgCenter released the Beauregard, an orange fleshed variety that went on to be grown far beyond the state. The Thanksgiving pairing with marshmallow is younger than the crop: the earliest known printed recipe for mashed sweet potatoes baked under marshmallows is in a 1917 booklet that the Angelus Marshmallow company commissioned to find new uses for its marshmallows.

new.definition: Nuts coated in cooked sugar that sets hard and crisp around each one. Some are tossed in a sugar syrup that dries to a sandy crust, others in sugar taken to caramel, which sets in a glassy amber shell. The coating brings sweetness and snap against the soft richness of the nut. On the Thanksgiving Day menu they were candied pecans on the Sweet Potato Agnolotti and candied hazelnuts on the Chocolate and Orange Tart.
new.guest: Candied nuts are nuts cooked in sugar until each one wears a crisp, sweet coat. On Thanksgiving Day there were candied pecans on the sweet potato agnolotti, a sweet crunch against the brown butter and goat cheese, and candied hazelnuts on the chocolate and orange tart.
new.kitchen: Candied nuts are cooled spread apart, so they set crisp and separate rather than in one clump. How the house candied its pecans and hazelnuts was the kitchen’s to say, and every nut question goes to the kitchen and the service note.
new.compare: The New Orleans praline is its nearest neighbor: a praline is a soft, creamy patty of pecans set in brown sugar, butter and cream, while candied nuts are single nuts, each in its own crisp coat. The candied nut is in fact closer to the first French praline, a whole almond in caramelized sugar.

new.background: The line of sugared nuts that leads to New Orleans begins with the French praline. The first pralines were whole almonds coated in caramelized sugar, and tradition names them for César de Choiseul, duc du Plessis-Praslin (1598 to 1675), whose cook is said to have made them, a story told often and never proven. A New Orleans story credits the Ursuline nuns, who came to the city in the eighteenth century, with bringing the candy, though 64 Parishes treats that story as legend. African American cooks in the kitchens of the French colonists, with pecans growing all around them, put pecans in place of almonds and added milk, and the praline turned into the soft, creamy patty the city knows. A single candied pecan, crisp in its own coat of sugar, keeps closer to the original French sweet.
